arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: General Verrilli argued the statute should not cover foreign corporate conduct abroad. He stated there is no meaningful connection to the United States in these cases.
Ms. Sullivan emphasized the case involves Nigerian plaintiffs suing an English and Dutch company. She noted the alleged conduct took place entirely within Nigeria.
Mr. Hoffman stated the plaintiffs received asylum in the United States. He argued they sued the defendants for their role in these human rights violations in U.S. courts.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case tests the reach of the Alien Tort Statute. It asks if U.S. courts can adjudicate claims about foreign corporate conduct abroad. The dispute centers on jurisdiction and international law application.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: The plaintiffs want a U.S. court to hear their human rights claims. They argue their asylum status creates a sufficient connection to the United States.
The defendants want the court to dismiss the case. They argue the conduct occurred entirely in Nigeria and lacks a meaningful U.S. connection.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The plaintiffs argue their presence in the U.S. as asylum seekers links the case to American soil. They contend the statute allows suits for foreign conduct when plaintiffs are here.
The defendants argue the statute does not cover extraterritorial conduct by foreign corporations. They state there is no meaningful connection to the United States in this category of cases.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Ginsburg asked if personal jurisdiction was raised as a defense.

Justice Kennedy asked if a U.S. corporation can be sued globally for domestic violations. He also asked what U.S. effects exist between the Nigerian events and the U.S. connection claimed by the plaintiffs. Justice Scalia asked who decides what constitutes a violation of international law norms. Chief Justice Roberts asked if plaintiffs can sue in multiple countries simultaneously.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: The outcome defines the geographic limits of U.S. judicial power. It determines whether American courts adjudicate foreign corporate conduct abroad. This shapes the role of U.S. courts in international human rights enforcement. It clarifies the scope of the Alien Tort Statute for foreign actors.
